If some sentence is true, then all later ones are false; but any later sentence’s claim about still later sentences creates pressure for a true one. If none is true, then each sentence’s claim that all later ones are false appears true. The construction challenges whether self-reference is essential to semantic paradox, though the sequence as a whole has indirect global dependence.
paradoxes.origin: Stephen Yablo introduced the sequence in a 1993 paper on paradox without self-reference.

examples.text: S1 says all later sentences are false, S2 says the same of those after it, and the pattern continues forever.
examples.note: No sentence directly mentions itself, but the infinite sequence is globally entangled.

commonMisreadings: It does not settle whether indirect dependence counts as a form of self-reference.
criticisms: Formal analyses differ on the role of infinitary semantics and on which truth principles should be retained.

paradoxes.name: Zeno's paradoxes
paradoxes.summary: Zeno's arguments use apparently plausible claims about motion or plurality to derive an infinite regress or contradiction.
paradoxes.body:
Zeno's paradoxes challenge how motion and plurality can be understood. In the dichotomy argument, a traveler must reach halfway, then half the remaining distance, and so on, apparently requiring infinitely many stages before arriving. The Achilles argument applies this structure to a faster runner pursuing a slower one.

Modern mathematics models infinite convergent series, allowing infinitely many diminishing intervals to sum to a finite distance; this addresses the standard mathematical form but does not settle every philosophical question about motion, space, or time. Zeno's arguments have multiple versions and interpretations. They should not be reduced to the claim that motion is visibly impossible.
paradoxes.origin: Attributed to Zeno of Elea in ancient Greece; several arguments are reported by Aristotle and later commentators.

examples.text: To cross a room, a person must first travel half the distance, then half of what remains, producing endlessly many smaller segments.
examples.note: The paradox asks how an infinite division can be completed in finite time.

examples.text: Achilles reaches each point where the tortoise previously stood, while the tortoise moves ahead; the sequence of catch-up points is infinite.
examples.note: The apparent failure to overtake comes from treating each stage as a barrier.

commonMisreadings: The argument is not a simple denial of observed motion; it challenges assumptions about infinite divisibility and completing infinitely many stages.
Convergence of a series resolves a mathematical representation, but philosophical interpretations of the paradox continue.
criticisms: Critics argue that the argument equivocates between a completed infinite division and an endless process, or misrepresents time and distance.

paradoxes.name: Zermelo recurrence paradox
paradoxes.summary: A finite isolated mechanical system may eventually return arbitrarily close to an earlier state, apparently conflicting with irreversible entropy increase.
paradoxes.body: Poincaré recurrence implies that a bounded conservative system with suitable finite phase-space measure will return arbitrarily near its initial state after enough time. Zermelo argued that such recurrence sits uneasily with Boltzmann’s account of entropy increase. The timescales for macroscopic systems are immense, and recurrence does not prevent entropy from increasing for overwhelmingly typical intervals. The issue asks how statistical irreversibility relates to reversible dynamics and recurrence.
paradoxes.origin: Ernst Zermelo used Poincaré’s recurrence theorem to challenge Boltzmann’s kinetic theory in 1896.

examples.text: A gas may eventually return close to a low-entropy arrangement even though it ordinarily spreads and remains dispersed for vast periods.
examples.note: Recurrence is compatible with overwhelmingly long intervals spent near equilibrium.

commonMisreadings: It is not an observation that a room’s air will practically gather in one corner.
criticisms: The theorem’s assumptions and the distinction between exact and approximate recurrence matter.
